```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(cowplot)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(viridis)

library(stringr)
```

## Learning goals

1. Analyze a single categorical variable using the [binomial test]{.alert}, a type of null hypothesis significance test
2. Determine when to use a binomial test
3. Estimate uncertainty of a proportion

## Orange M&Ms

According to Mars Chocolate North America, 20% of Milk Chocolate M&Ms are [orange]{.alert}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](/img/orange-mm.jpg){width="80%" fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
::: {.pause-think}
If you sample 3 M&Ms at random from a bag, what is the probability you have exactly 1 [orange]{.alert} M&M?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Pr[1 of 3 M&Ms is [orange]{.alert}] = `r dbinom(1, 3, 0.2)`
:::

:::

:::


## Pr[1 of 3 M&Ms is [orange]{.alert}]

Using a [probability tree]{.alert} can help!

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "10in"

df_tree <- tibble(
    x = c(rep(0, 2), rep(2, 4), rep(4, 8)),
    y = c(rep(0, 2), rep(c(-2, 2), each = 2), rep(c(-3, -1, 1, 3), each = 2)),
    xend = x + 1,
    yend = c(-2, 2, -3, -1, 1, 3, -3.5, -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5)
)

df_label <- tibble(
    x = rep(c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5), c(2, 4, 8)),
    y = c(-2, 2, -3, -1, 1, 3, -3.5, -2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5),
    color = rep(c("orange", "not orange"), 7),
    prob = rep(c("0.2", "0.8"), 7)
)

df_summary <- tidyr::crossing(
    prob1 = c(0.2, 0.8), prob2 = c(0.2, 0.8), prob3 = c(0.2, 0.8)
) |>
    mutate(
        x = 7,
        y = seq(-3.5, 3.5, 1),
        prob = glue("{prob1} %*% {prob2} %*% {prob3}")
    ) |>
    rowwise() |>
    summarize(
        x = x, y = y,
        prob = prob,
        n_orange = sum(c_across(matches("^prob[1-3]$")) == 0.2))

gp <- ggplot(df_tree, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    xlim(-1, 8.5) + ylim(-4, 4) +
    geom_segment(size = 1.2) +
    geom_point(
        data = df_label,
        mapping = aes(x, y, fill = color), shape = 21,
        inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 6
    ) +
    geom_text(
        data = df_label,
        mapping = aes(x - 1, y, label = prob),
        inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 6
    ) +
    annotate("text", x = c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5), y= 4, label = str_c("M&M ", 1:3),
             size = 6) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "orange")) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size=10))) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 18)
    )

gp
```

## Pr[1 of 3 M&Ms is [orange]{.alert}]

Calculate probability of each outcome

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10

#| out-width: "10in"

gp +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6)
```


## Pr[1 of 3 M&Ms is [orange]{.alert}]

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="0" style="text-align: left; width: 100%;"}
Count the ways to get desired outcome
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="0" style="text-align: left; width: 100%;"}
Add up probabilities: $3 \times (0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.8) = `r dbinom(1, 3, 0.2)`$
:::

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "10in"

gp +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey", "black")) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x + 1.5, y, label = n_orange, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE

```

## Orange M&Ms

What is the probability of sampling 4 [orange]{.alert} M&Ms from a bag of 20 if $p = 0.2$ orange?

::: {.fragment}
Drawing a probability tree would be too hard.
:::

::: {.fragment}
"Fortunately" there's an equation!
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\text{Pr}[X~\text{successes in}~n~\text{trials}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$
:::


## Binomial distribution {.top-align}

$$\text{Pr}[X~\text{successes in}~n~\text{trials}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$


- ${n \choose X}$: a count of the number of ways you could get $X$ successes in $n$ trials
- $p^X$: the probability of $X$ "successes" (multiplication rule)
- $(1-p)^{n-X}$: the probability of $n - X$ "failures" (multiplication rule)


## Binomial distribution

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="20%"}
Same same!
:::

::: {.column width="20%"}
${n \choose X} = 3$
:::

::: {.column width="20%"}
$p^X = 0.2$
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
$(1-p)^{n-X} = 0.8 \times 0.8$
:::

:::

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "10in"

gp +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x, y, label = prob, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, parse = TRUE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey", "black")) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y= 4, label = "Probability", size = 6) +
  geom_text(
    data = df_summary,
    mapping = aes(x + 1.5, y, label = n_orange, color = n_orange == 1),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.5, y= 4, label = "italic(N)[orange]", size = 6, parse = TRUE) +
  NULL
```

## Binomial distribution (graphically) {.top-align}

What is the probability of sampling $X$ [orange]{.alert} M&Ms from a bag of 20?

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="25%"}
$p = 0.2$

$n = 20$ trials



:::


::: {.column width="75%"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="1"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"

df <- tidyr::crossing(
    n = 20,
    `X successes` = 0:20,
    p = 0.2
) |>
    mutate(Probability = dbinom(`X successes`, n, p))

gp <- ggplot(df, aes(`X successes`, Probability)) +
    geom_col(fill = "tomato") +
    xlab(expression(paste(italic(X), " orange M&Ms"))) +
    theme_cowplot()

gp
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "5in"

gp  +
    geom_col(data = filter(df, `X successes` == 4), 
             aes(`X successes`, Probability), 
             fill = "black", 
             inherit.aes = FALSE)
```
:::

:::

:::

:::

::: {.absolute top="500" left="0"}

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
$$
\begin{align}
\text{Pr}[4~\text{orange}~M\&Ms] &= {20 \choose 4} 0.2^4 (1 - 0.2)^{(20 - 4)} \\
&\approx 0.218
\end{align}
$$
:::

:::

```{r}
df <- tidyr::crossing(

```

## Binomial distribution

> The **binomial distribution** provides the probability distribution for the number of "successes" in a fixed number of independent trials, when the probability of success is the same in each trial.

Assumptions:

* the number of trials ($n$) is fixed
* separate trials are independent, and
* the probability of "success" ($p$) is the same in every trial

## Binomial distribution

$$\text{Pr}[X~\textit{successes}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$

- ${n \choose X}$: a count of the number of ways you could get $X$ successes in $n$ trials
- $p^X$: the probability of $X$ "successes" (multiplication rule)
- $(1-p)^{n-X}$: the probability of $n - X$ "failures" (multiplication rule)




## Binomial distribution (in code)

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$p = 0.2$

$n = 20$ trials

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "5in"


df <- tidyr::crossing(
  n = 20,
  `X successes` = 0:20,
  p = 0.2
) |>
  mutate(Probability = dbinom(`X successes`, n, p))

ggplot(df, aes(`X successes`, Probability)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ p, labeller = label_bquote(cols = italic(p) == .(p))) +
  geom_col(fill = "tomato") +
  xlab(expression(paste(italic(X), " orange M&Ms"))) +
  theme_cowplot()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
What is $Pr(X = 1)$?

```{r}
#| echo: true

dbinom(1, size = 20, p = 0.2)
```

What is $Pr(X \leq 1)$?

```{r}
#| echo: true

pbinom(1, size = 20, p = 0.2)
```
:::
:::

## Summary

The [binomial distribution]{.alert} describes the probability of all possible outcomes from $n$ trials with probability of success $p$

Therefore, it is a [sampling distribution]{.alert} from a sample size of $n$ from a population where a proportion $p$ of the population is one discrete value (e.g. orange)

## M&Ms are fun and all...

But what are some biologically relevant examples?

::: {.incremental}
- Does a certain species prefer one habitat over another? [test statistic:]{.alert} number of occurrences in first habitat type versus the other
- Is a certain class of gene clustered on one chromosome? [test statistic:]{.alert} count of genes in the class on a specific chromosome versus all other chromosomes
- What is the dietary preference of some species? [test statistic:]{.alert} count of times the species ate one food type versus another
:::

## Food preferences of the peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha

**Question:** Do peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha prefer māmaki over plants in the *Urtica* genus?

**Scientific hypothesis:** Yes, peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha prefer māmaki over plants in the *Urtica* genus

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Conduct a feeding trial**

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="0"}
::: {.pause-think}
What are $H_0$ and $H_A$?
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="0"}
- $H_0$: The proportion of times peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha choose māmaki versus *Urtica* will be 0.5
- $H_A$: The proportion of times peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha choose māmaki versus *Urtica* will not be 0.5
:::

:::


:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](/img/feeding_trial.png){width="80%" fig-align="center"}

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
4. Calculate the $P$-value
5. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $\le \alpha$
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $> \alpha$

## $H_0$ and $H_A$ deal with [proportions]{.alert}

> A [proportion]{.alert} is the fraction of individuals having a particular attribute.

$$p = \frac{\text{Number of "successes"}}{\text{Number of trials}}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Example:** 21 out of 30 peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha chose māmaki over *Urtica*, so the [estimated]{.alert} proportion is $\frac{21}{30}=0.7$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Note: The true proportion is a [population parameter]{.alert}, and we can [estimate]{.alert} it from data
:::

## Parameter and estimate

 Parameter | Estimate
:---------:|:--------:
 $p$       | $\hat{p}$

- $H_A$: The proportion of times peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha choose māmaki versus *Urtica* will not be 0.5
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="0"}
- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
:::

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller


- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$

::: {.fragment}
- [Test statistic]{.alert}: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
:::

::: {.fragment}

::: {.pause-think}
What is the [null distribution]{.alert}?
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
The null distribution is the [binomial distribution]{.alert} with $p = 0.5$
:::


## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
$p = 0.5$

$n = 30$ trials

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 2
#| out-width: "5in"


df <- tidyr::crossing(
    n = 30,
    `X successes` = 0:30,
    p = 0.5
) |>
    mutate(Probability = dbinom(`X successes`, n, p))

ggplot(df, aes(`X successes`, Probability)) +
    geom_col(fill = "gray") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    geom_col(data = filter(df, `X successes` >= 21 | `X successes` <= 9), 
             aes(`X successes`, Probability, fill = "tomato"), 
             inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}


```{r}
#| echo: true

# number of trials
n <- 30 

# number of times chose māmaki
x_success <- 21 

# null hypothesis proportion
p <- 0.5 

# P-value
upper <- pbinom(x_success - 1, size = n, prob = p,
                lower.tail = FALSE)

lower <- pbinom(n - x_success, size = n, prob = p,
                lower.tail = TRUE)

pval <- upper + lower

pval
```

:::

:::

## Food preferences of the peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha

- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
- Test statistic: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
- The null distribution is the [binomial distribution]{.alert} with $p = 0.5$

::: {.fragment}
- With $P$-value = `r round(pval, 3)` we **reject** the null at $\alpha = 0.05$ significance
:::


## Confidence Interval of a proportion

Remember, $\hat{p}$ (the proportion) is a sample estimate of the population parameter. Like any estimate we can calculate a confidence interval. But...

::: {.fragement}
The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution.
:::

## Confidence Interval of a proportion

The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution. So...

::: {.fragment}

We use R code instead

```{r}
#| echo: true

n <- 30
x_success <- 21

# P-value and 95% CI
binom.test(x_success, n)
```

:::
